title: Salsabila and the Sparkling Sea
blurb: Strange blue lights dance on the water near the island, and nobody agrees what they are. Salsabila decides to find out.

chapters.title: Lights on the Water
chapters.text:
The island of Pulau Lerang was so small that Salsabila could walk around it before lunch. Her grandmother, Nenek, sold dried fish at the harbour, and every evening Salsabila sat on the end of the old wooden jetty, watching the sky turn orange. She knew every boat by the sound of its engine. When the fishing boats went out at dusk, she counted their lamps as they spread across the eastern water. There were always eleven.

On the third night of the school holidays, she stayed out later than usual, because the house was too hot for sleeping. Then she noticed something strange. Far out beyond the rocks, tiny blue lights flickered on the black water. She counted the boat lamps first. Eleven, all of them to the east, just where they should be.

These lights were something else. They did not move like boat lamps. They sparkled and faded, like stars falling into the sea. When a wave broke over the rocks, a line of blue ran along it and was gone.

"Nenek, come and see!" she called.

Nenek came slowly along the planks, wiping her hands on her sarong. She stood on the jetty for a long time, her hand shading her eyes, although there was no sun to shade them from.

"I have lived here for seventy years," she said slowly. "I have never seen that."

She said it very quietly, and that frightened Salsabila more than a shout would have done. Nenek knew when the squid were running and which clouds meant rain. She knew this sea as well as she knew her own kitchen.

Salsabila's best friend Galih came running along the planks, his sandals slapping. "The fishermen are talking about it," he panted. "Some of the boats have seen it too. They say it is a bad sign."

"A sign of what?" asked Salsabila.

Galih shrugged. "Nobody knows. That is why it is bad."

Behind them, torches were moving along the harbour, and people were talking in low voices. Out on the water, the blue lights flickered and died and flickered again. Salsabila did not feel afraid, exactly. She felt the way she felt when a sum would not come out, a kind of itch at the back of her mind. Those lights had a reason, and she wanted to know what it was.

questions.prompt: Why was the island easy to walk around?
options: It was very small
It had a good road around it
It was joined to the mainland
It was flat and empty
questions.why: The island was so small that Salsabila could walk around it before lunch.

questions.prompt: How did Salsabila know that the blue lights were not fishing boats?
options: She could hear that the engines of all the boats had been turned off
Her grandmother had told her that no boats went out in the third week
All eleven boat lamps were somewhere else, and the blue lights moved differently
Boats were not allowed to go out to sea on the nights of the holidays
questions.why: She counted eleven boat lamps to the east, where they should be, and the blue lights did not move like boat lamps.

questions.prompt: How did the lights behave?
options: They moved in straight lines like lamps
They sparkled and faded like falling stars
They rose up slowly into the sky
They stayed still and shone steadily
questions.why: They sparkled and faded, like stars falling into the sea.

questions.prompt: What happened when a wave broke over the rocks?
options: A great cloud of white steam rose from the water
The rocks began to shine with a yellow light
The lights all went out for the rest of the night
A line of blue ran along it and was gone
questions.why: When a wave broke over the rocks, a line of blue ran along it and was gone.

questions.prompt: Why did Nenek's quiet words frighten Salsabila?
options: Nenek had told her that a storm was on its way to the island
Nenek knew the sea very well, yet even she had never seen this
Nenek had said that she would have to leave the jetty at once
Nenek hardly ever spoke to her in such a quiet voice
questions.why: The text says Nenek knew the sea as well as she knew her own kitchen. If she had not seen it in seventy years, it was truly strange.

questions.prompt: What do the fishermen think the lights mean?
options: A bad sign
A big catch
Good luck
A coming ship
questions.why: Galih reports what they say: "They say it is a bad sign."

questions.prompt: What does Galih's answer "That is why it is bad" suggest about people's fear?
options: People are only pretending to be afraid in order to tease him
People have seen the lights cause harm many times before
People are afraid because they do not understand the lights
People have been told by a scientist that the lights are dangerous
questions.why: He says nobody knows what it is a sign of, and that is why it is bad. The fear comes from not knowing.

questions.prompt: How does Salsabila feel at the end of the chapter?
options: Bored, and keen to go home to bed
Terrified, and ready to run back to the house
Angry, because Galih will not explain it
Curious, like when a sum will not come out
questions.why: She felt the way she felt when a sum would not come out, a kind of itch at the back of her mind, and she wanted to know the reason.

chapters.title: What the Elders Said
chapters.text:
The next morning, the whole harbour was buzzing. No boats had stayed out past midnight, and the nets lay in heaps. Pak Haji, the oldest fisherman, sat on an upturned boat with his arms crossed. When he spoke, men listened.

"In my grandfather's time," he said, "there were lights like these before a great wave. We must not take the boats out."

Some men nodded. Others shook their heads. A day without fishing was a day without money, and everyone there knew it.

"It is only a trick of the moon," said a young fisherman called Rudi. His ears had turned red, but he went on. "My children cannot eat an old story."

"There was no moon last night," somebody called. Then everybody was talking at once.

Salsabila listened carefully from behind the drying racks, where she was helping Nenek to turn the fish. She liked Pak Haji. He had taught her to tie a bowline when she was six. She knew that old stories had kept boats off the rocks for longer than anyone could remember. She was not going to laugh at him. But she also liked finding things out for herself. At school, her science teacher Bu Dewi often said, "Do not argue about a mystery. Collect evidence."

She looked around. The harbour was full of opinions this morning. But nobody had written down what time the lights had come, or where they were, or what they did. Nobody had been anywhere near them.

"Galih," she said quietly, "I do not think the lights are a warning. I think they are something we can study. Do you have your notebook?"

Galih grinned. From his back pocket he pulled a damp, bent notebook held together with a rubber band. He wrote everything in it: football scores, the times of the ferry, the names of Nenek's cats.

"I always do," he said.

Nenek turned another fish, and she did not look up. "Be careful that you do not make Pak Haji look foolish," she said. "That old man was bringing boats home safely before your mother was born."

"I know, Nek," said Salsabila. "If he turns out to be right, I will be the first to say so."

questions.prompt: Who is Pak Haji?
options: The teacher at the island's school
The doctor who visits from the mainland
The oldest fisherman on the island
The owner of the drying racks
questions.why: Pak Haji, the oldest fisherman, sat on an upturned boat with his arms crossed.

questions.prompt: What does Pak Haji say should happen?
options: The boats should stay in because a great wave may come
The fish should be salted and sold before the rain comes
The children should stay away from the end of the jetty
The lights should be studied by a scientist from the city
questions.why: He says there were lights like these before a great wave, and "We must not take the boats out."

questions.prompt: Why does Rudi argue against Pak Haji?
options: He has seen the same lights in many other seas
He has read a science book about the lights
He wants to be chosen as the new head of the harbour
A day without fishing would leave his family without money
questions.why: He says, "My children cannot eat an old story." The text also says a day without fishing was a day without money.

questions.prompt: What is the weak point in Rudi's idea about the moon?
options: Moonlight is not able to reach the sea
There was no moon last night
The moon is never out in the holidays
The moon shines only on the rocks
questions.why: Somebody called out, "There was no moon last night." So moonlight could not have caused the lights.

questions.prompt: What does Salsabila think is missing from the harbour argument?
options: Fish, because the nets are lying in heaps on the sand
Time, because the boats have to go out before midday
Evidence, such as when and where the lights appeared
Respect, because everyone is shouting at the old men
questions.why: The harbour was full of opinions, but nobody had written down what time the lights had come, or where they were, or what they did.

questions.prompt: How does Salsabila feel about Pak Haji?
options: She fears him and will not go anywhere near him
She dislikes him and hopes to prove that he is a fool
She agrees with him and wants all the boats to stay in
She respects him, but she still wants to test the idea
questions.why: She liked him and was not going to laugh at him. But she also liked finding things out for herself.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best describes Galih's notebook?
options: He uses it to write down all kinds of things
He has just bought it from the shop on the harbour
He keeps it only for his science homework
He has never written anything in it before
questions.why: He wrote everything in it: football scores, the times of the ferry, the names of Nenek's cats.

questions.prompt: Why does Nenek warn Salsabila about making Pak Haji look foolish?
options: She believes that the lights really will bring a great wave
He has earned respect, and she does not want it taken from him in public
She is afraid that he will stop buying dried fish from her stall
She does not want her granddaughter to study science at all
questions.why: She says he was bringing boats home safely before Salsabila's mother was born. That long record is why he deserves care.

chapters.title: A Plan for Midnight
chapters.text:
That afternoon, the friends sat on the jetty with a pencil and a chart. Salsabila had drawn the rocks and the bay from memory. Then they went around asking everyone who had seen the lights: the fishermen, the ice seller, the cook on the ferry. Each time, they asked the same two questions. When did you see them? Where were you?

Galih marked each answer on the chart. He had noticed that the lights had appeared at about nine o'clock, and again around midnight. Salsabila noticed something else. Nearly all the marks were by the rocks, or close behind a moving boat. Hardly any were in the still water of the bay.

"If we want to see them closely," said Salsabila, "we must go out. We need a boat."

"Nenek's little canoe has no engine," said Galih. "We can paddle quietly. That is better, anyway. A motor might scare away whatever it is."

Salsabila wrote a list: torch, notebook, a glass jar with a lid, two life jackets, a rope and a thermos of warm tea.

"Why a jar?" asked Galih.

"Evidence," she said. "We are going to bring back a piece of the mystery."

"And why tea?"

"In case the mystery takes a long time."

Then she frowned. It would be easy to slip out after Nenek had gone to sleep. She looked at Galih, and she could see that he was thinking the same thing. She tapped the pencil against her teeth.

"We need to tell an adult," she said. "Rule number one, even for scientists."

So she asked Nenek, who was mending a net in the last of the light. Nenek thought about it for a long time, while the net needle went in and out. She asked how far they would go, and what they would do if the wind changed. Salsabila had answers to both.

"You may go," she said at last, "but you will stay close to the jetty light, and I will sit at the end with my torch. If I flash it three times, you come straight back, and you do not argue."

Before dark, Pak Haji walked down the beach to look at the canoe. He said nothing to anyone. He looked at it for some time, retied one of the knots, and walked slowly away.

questions.prompt: What did the friends use to record the reports?
options: A pencil and a chart
A phone and a camera
A computer and a printer
A tape recorder and a map
questions.why: The friends sat on the jetty with a pencil and a chart, and Galih marked each answer on the chart.

questions.prompt: At what times had the lights appeared?
options: Only at dawn on the third day
At about nine o'clock and around midnight
At sunrise and again around noon
At noon and again at three o'clock
questions.why: He had noticed that the lights had appeared at about nine o'clock, and again around midnight.

questions.prompt: What pattern did Salsabila notice on the chart?
options: Most lights were seen by people who had not been out in boats
Most lights were in the still water of the bay, far from boats
Most lights were where the water was moving, by rocks or boats
Most lights came on nights when the wind was blowing from the east
questions.why: Nearly all the marks were by the rocks, or close behind a moving boat. Hardly any were in the still water of the bay.

questions.prompt: Why did the friends choose a canoe without an engine?
options: A motor could not be used during the night
A motor would have been too heavy to carry
A motor would have cost far too much money
A motor might scare away whatever it was
questions.why: Galih said, "We can paddle quietly. A motor might scare away whatever it is."

questions.prompt: Which item is not on Salsabila's list?
options: A rope
Life jackets
A glass jar
A fishing net
questions.why: The list had a torch, notebook, glass jar with a lid, two life jackets, a rope and a thermos of warm tea.

questions.prompt: Why did Salsabila want to take a jar?
options: To bring back a sample of the mystery as evidence
To hold the rope and keep it dry in the canoe
To catch some small fish for Nenek's market stall
To keep a supply of fresh drinking water with them
questions.why: She says, "Evidence. We are going to bring back a piece of the mystery."

questions.prompt: Why did Salsabila tell Nenek, although slipping out would have been easy?
options: She had forgotten where Nenek kept the paddles for the canoe
She knew that going out at night needed an adult's agreement for safety
She wanted Nenek to come out in the canoe and paddle for them
She knew that Nenek would certainly catch her if she tried to go
questions.why: She says, "We need to tell an adult. Rule number one, even for scientists."

questions.prompt: What does Pak Haji's visit to the canoe show?
options: He is trying to stop the children by damaging the knots
He has decided that the lights are nothing to be afraid of
He may not agree with them, but he cares about their safety
He is planning to take the canoe out on his own that night
questions.why: He says nothing and reties a knot to make the canoe safer. He has warned against going out, yet he still looks after them.

chapters.title: The Water That Glowed
chapters.text:
At ten minutes to midnight, the friends pushed the canoe from the beach. The sea was dark and calm. There was no moon, only the jetty light behind them like a small yellow star. They paddled slowly, and each time the paddle dipped, something wonderful happened. The water around the blade burst into a cloud of tiny blue sparks, like glitter lit from inside. When Salsabila lifted the paddle, every drop that fell made its own small ring of light.

"Look!" whispered Galih. He trailed his hand through the water. Glowing swirls streamed from his fingers. A fish shot under the canoe like a blue comet, leaving a bright line behind it, and he nearly dropped his notebook.

For a moment, neither of them said anything. Salsabila held her breath. All her life she had looked at this water, and she had never known that it could do this.

"There is no ghost here," she said softly. "The sea itself is glowing."

Then she remembered why they had come. "Time," she said.

Galih looked at his watch. "Two minutes to midnight."

"Write it down. And what does the water feel like?"

He put his hand in again. "Warm. Warmer than usual, like a bath that someone has left standing."

She dipped her jar and lifted it. Inside the water, a thousand tiny dots glowed each time the jar moved, and dimmed when it stood still. She held it very still, and it went dark. She tapped the glass with one finger, and a small light woke up. She shook it hard, and for a moment she was holding a blue lamp in her hand. Her heart was beating very fast.

"They shine when they are disturbed," she said. "That is why the lights flashed near the rocks. The waves were moving them. And that is why the boats saw them too. Their engines were stirring up the water."

"Are they alive?" asked Galih.

"I do not know," she said, and she screwed on the lid. "But Bu Dewi will."

Far away on the jetty, a torch blinked twice. Nenek was watching. Galih lifted their own torch and blinked twice in reply.

They turned the canoe towards home, and every stroke of the paddles drew a line of blue fire behind them, all the way to the shore.

questions.prompt: What happened when the paddle dipped into the water?
options: The canoe stopped moving and started to spin
The water around the canoe became very hot
Tiny blue sparks appeared around the blade
A large fish jumped straight out of the sea
questions.why: The water around the blade burst into a cloud of tiny blue sparks.

questions.prompt: Why did the fish look like a blue comet?
options: It leapt high out of the sea and across the night sky
Its movement through the water made a bright line behind it
It had blue scales that shone in the light of the torch
It was carrying a small piece of the jetty light with it
questions.why: A fish shot under the canoe, leaving a bright line behind it. A comet is a bright object with a tail of light.

questions.prompt: What did Salsabila realise when she saw the glow around them?
options: The light was coming from a ghost in the water
The light was only a trick of the moon
The light was coming from a boat far away
The light was coming from the sea water itself
questions.why: She said, "There is no ghost here. The sea itself is glowing."

questions.prompt: Why did Salsabila suddenly say "Time"?
options: She remembered they had come to collect evidence
She could not read her watch in the dark
She wanted to know when they should have their tea
She was afraid they would be late for Nenek's signal
questions.why: The text says she remembered why they had come. Writing down the time and the feel of the water is collecting evidence.

questions.prompt: When did the dots in the jar glow?
options: Only when the torch was on
When the jar was moved or tapped
Only when the lid was on
When the jar stood very still
questions.why: A thousand tiny dots glowed each time the jar moved, and dimmed when it stood still. She tapped it, and a small light woke up.

questions.prompt: Why did the lights flash near the rocks?
options: The waves were disturbing the tiny glowing things
The fish were chasing each other around the rocks
The moon was shining brightly down on the rocks
The rocks were hot from the heat of the sun
questions.why: She said they shine when they are disturbed. "That is why the lights flashed near the rocks. The waves were moving them."

questions.prompt: How does the jar test fit with what Salsabila noticed on the chart in chapter three?
options: Both show that the light is strongest in the still bay
Both show that the light appears only at exactly midnight
Both show that the light appears where the water is being moved
Both show that the light comes from the jetty lamp
questions.why: The chart showed most lights near rocks and boats, and in the jar the dots glow when moved and go dark when still.

questions.prompt: Why was two blinks of the torch not a problem for the children?
options: Two blinks meant that the tea was ready at home
The torch was too far away to see at all
Nenek had told them to ignore her torch all night
Nenek's signal to come back at once was three flashes
questions.why: In chapter three she said that if she flashed three times, they had to come straight back. Two blinks only showed that she was watching.

chapters.title: Bu Dewi Explains
chapters.text:
In the morning, Salsabila carried the jar to the empty school. It was the holidays, but Bu Dewi lived in the little house next door, and she came over at once. She put a few drops under the school's one microscope, and her eyebrows rose.

"Beautiful," she said. She let each of them look. At first Salsabila saw only a grey blur. Then she turned the knob, and tiny round shapes came swimming into view, like clear balloons with little tails.

"These are called dinoflagellates," said Bu Dewi. "They are single-celled living things, so small that you cannot see one without a microscope. But when many of them gather, they make the water glow. Some people call them sea sparkle."

"Why do they glow?" asked Galih, writing as fast as he could.

"Scientists think the light is a defence," said Bu Dewi. "When a tiny animal tries to eat them, the flash may attract a bigger animal that eats the attacker. It is a bit like a burglar alarm in a shop. This glowing is called bioluminescence. Many deep-sea creatures also make their own light, and so do fireflies on land."

"So, is it a bad sign?" asked Salsabila. She thought of the old man on the upturned boat. "Pak Haji says there were lights like these before a great wave."

Bu Dewi took her time to answer. "It is a sign that the sea is alive," she said. "Large groups like this often appear when the water is warm and full of nutrients. Nothing in that jar can know that a wave is coming. But I was not there in his grandfather's time. Perhaps there were lights one year, and a wave soon after, and people remembered them together. When two things happen close together, it is natural to think that one caused the other. That does not make it so."

Galih looked up. "So how long will it last?"

"It will pass in a few days. And Pak Haji is right about one thing. People should watch the sea carefully when it changes. Some kinds of these tiny living things can make shellfish unsafe to eat, so I would leave the shellfish alone until it has gone."

Salsabila looked down at the jar in her hands. "How do I tell him?" she asked.

Bu Dewi smiled and picked up the microscope. "Carefully," she said. "And I think you should let him look for himself."

questions.prompt: What did Bu Dewi use to look at the water?
options: A telescope
A torch
A microscope
A camera
questions.why: She put a few drops under the school's one microscope.

questions.prompt: What did the tiny living things look like under the microscope?
options: Tiny stars with five points
Clear balloons with little tails
Grey stones with sharp edges
Small blue fish with long fins
questions.why: Tiny round shapes came swimming into view, like clear balloons with little tails.

questions.prompt: What does single-celled mean?
options: Made of many parts
Living for one day
Found in one place
Made of just one cell
questions.why: They are single-celled living things. The word single means one, so each is made of one cell.

questions.prompt: Why might these creatures glow, according to scientists?
options: The flash may attract a bigger animal that eats the attacker
The light may show other fish where they are sleeping
The light may help them to see where the food is at night
The glow may warm the water so that they can grow faster
questions.why: Scientists think the light is a defence. The flash may attract a bigger animal that eats the attacker.

questions.prompt: Why does Bu Dewi compare the glow to a burglar alarm?
options: Both are switched on by a person at the end of each day
Both make a very loud noise when anyone comes near them
Both keep on working only when the weather is very warm
Both make a sudden signal that may bring something to catch the attacker
questions.why: An alarm goes off when a thief breaks in, and it brings help. The flash goes off when something attacks, and it may bring a bigger animal.

questions.prompt: What is the glowing of living things called?
options: Evaporation
Bioluminescence
Pollution
Reflection
questions.why: This glowing is called bioluminescence.

questions.prompt: How does Bu Dewi explain the old story about lights and a great wave?
options: The lights really did cause a great wave in those days
The great wave brought the glowing creatures to the island from far away
People may have linked two events that only happened close together
People must have made up the whole story to frighten small children
questions.why: She says perhaps there were lights one year, and a wave soon after, and people remembered them together. That does not mean one caused the other.

questions.prompt: What practical advice does Bu Dewi give until the glow has gone?
options: Leave the shellfish alone
Keep all the boats in harbour
Stay out of the water at night
Empty the jar back into the sea
questions.why: Some kinds can make shellfish unsafe to eat, so she would leave the shellfish alone until it has gone.

chapters.title: Keeping the Secret
chapters.text:
By evening, the news had spread across Pulau Lerang. Salsabila carried the jar down to the upturned boat herself, and her mouth was dry. All the men were there. She did not tell Pak Haji that he was wrong. She told him what they had seen, what they had written down and what Bu Dewi had said. Then Bu Dewi set up the microscope on the boat, and the old man bent over it for a long time.

Nobody spoke. Pak Haji tapped the jar with one fingernail and watched the small light wake. He stroked his chin. At last he said, "I am old and I have lived by the old stories. But today I have learned something new. That is a good day."

He held up a finger. "But you will all still look at the sky before you go out."

"Yes, Pak," they said, and the fishermen laughed. Some of them clapped Salsabila on the back. Rudi gave her a lopsided grin. "You win," he said. "It was not the moon." That night, all the boats went out.

A few days later, the glow faded, just as Bu Dewi had said. But visitors had already begun to arrive in small boats, eager to see the sparkling sea. Someone had put pictures on the internet. More people came, and they stayed even when there was nothing left to see. They brought loud engines and plastic bottles, and one morning there was a rainbow film of oil on the water by the jetty.

At the harbour meeting, some people said that visitors meant money, and others said that they meant trouble. Salsabila stood up, and her knees were shaking. She had never spoken at a meeting before.

"It is lovely to share the sea," she said. "But we must keep it clean. No rubbish, no loud engines, no chemicals. Remember that the sea is a home for living things."

Rudi rubbed his neck. "If the lights come back," he said slowly, "people might pay to go out quietly in a canoe."

Everyone agreed. That night, the sea was quiet and dark again, and Salsabila sat at the end of the jetty with Nenek. She counted the boat lamps. Eleven. Perhaps the lights would come back next year, and perhaps not for another seventy years. Either way, Galih's notebook was ready. Salsabila smiled. She knew where to look for stars.

questions.prompt: How did Salsabila avoid making Pak Haji look foolish?
options: She asked Bu Dewi to explain everything for her
She told everyone that he had been right all along
She reported the evidence and let him look for himself
She waited until all of the other men had gone home
questions.why: She did not tell him he was wrong. She told him what they had seen and written down, and then he looked through the microscope himself.

questions.prompt: What does Pak Haji say about learning something new?
options: It is a waste of an old man's time
It is dangerous for people on the sea
It should be left to younger people
It makes for a good day
questions.why: He says, "Today I have learned something new. That is a good day."

questions.prompt: Why does Pak Haji add "you will all still look at the sky before you go out"?
options: He wants to stop all the boats from going out that night
The old knowledge of the sea is still useful, even with this new discovery
He is still sure that the blue lights will bring a great wave
He has decided that he no longer trusts the science teacher
questions.why: He has accepted the new idea, but he wants them to keep the old habits that keep boats safe. That night, all the boats go out.

questions.prompt: How does Rudi react to the news?
options: He cheerfully admits that his idea was wrong
He argues that it was the moon after all
He leaves the harbour and goes home angry
He tries to take the jar away from Salsabila
questions.why: Rudi gave her a lopsided grin and said, "You win. It was not the moon."

questions.prompt: Why did so many visitors keep coming?
options: Someone had put pictures of the sparkling sea on the internet
The fishermen had gone to the mainland to invite them
The ferry had started offering free trips to the island
The school had asked them to come and study the fish
questions.why: Visitors came to see the sparkling sea, and someone had put pictures on the internet. More people came.

questions.prompt: Which sign showed that the visitors were harming the sea?
options: A great number of fish in the fishermen's nets
A line of blue light along the top of the waves
A group of fireflies flying over the harbour
A rainbow film of oil on the water by the jetty
questions.why: They brought loud engines and plastic bottles, and one morning there was a rainbow film of oil on the water by the jetty.

questions.prompt: What rules does Salsabila suggest?
options: No fishing, no swimming, no canoes
No visitors, no boats, no pictures
No rubbish, no loud engines, no chemicals
No money, no ferry, no shellfish
questions.why: She says, "No rubbish, no loud engines, no chemicals."

questions.prompt: What does "She knew where to look for stars" mean at the end of the book?
options: She has learned how to find her way home at night by using the stars
She now knows the sea can hold its own lights, and she will watch for them
She has found a new place on the island to get a clear view of the sky
She has decided to give up science and study the night sky instead
questions.why: In chapter one, the lights looked like stars falling into the sea. Now she knows what they are, and that they may return.
